chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
title: Wettling the humorist and painter, pupil of Stuart Davis
summary: Wettling wrote the Esquire satire A Night Before Bopmas and painted under Stuart Davis; Freeman met De Kooning and other painters through him.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: As regards his music, he was a true artist all the way and he spent, you know, he became a session man, as we call it here, a studio man in the States. Did very well, but he had the drinking problem and then he did want to play jazz and of course, he worked down at Condon's for many, many years, but he was one of the funniest people I had ever met. He could make up things -- he
wrote a beautiful piece, you remember, that was published in Esquire, called A Night Before Bopmas, which was a satire on The Christmas Carol. You remember that?
Yes, I remember that. And he painted, too.

And he was a marvelous painter. He was a pupil of Stuart Davis, who became -- you know, Rockefeller paid $80,000 for a Stuart Davis, which is just as you walk up into the Museum of Modern Art in New York, I think the painting is still there. It's not exactly a painting. It looks like a rug.

Yes, and it's a Stuart Davis and I think given to the Museum by Rockefeller and anyway, Stuart Davis used to -- Stuart Davis taught George Wettling art, taught him how to paint for a short while, that is, he was with him but they were very close friends and Stuart Davis used to paint to jazz records.

Oh, yes, you take all the painters who knew -- I met all these painters through George Wettling, there was Pollack, there was the great Dutch-American painter who got, I understand a couple of years ago over $100,000 for a painting. I don't think any American painter ever received that. That was William De Kooning and I know his cousins who lived in The Hague, a
lovely house in The Hague, where I go to play.
